screens.title: HTTP Clients with requests and Advanced Features
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to move from low‑level socket work to a practical, human‑friendly HTTP client using the requests library. You will see how a few lines of code handle connection details, status codes, headers and JSON payloads, and how higher‑level features like sessions, authentication, timeouts, and streaming keep your applications reliable. For example, a single GET call can return JSON you parse immediately, while a session preserves cookies and reuses TCP connections to speed repeated requests. We will also cover common pitfalls: never ignoring status codes, always setting sensible timeouts, and avoiding disabling SSL verification in production. Practical examples include interacting with a public testing A P I to create, update, and delete resources, and a safe pattern for downloading very large files without exhausting memory. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design an HTTP client that is secure, efficient, and resilient to network problems. Think of requests as the reliable bridge between your Python code and web services — what will you build with that bridge?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when interacting with web services. First, you will master basic HTTP verbs and the common patterns for GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. Practically, that means you can fetch resources, create new ones, update existing records, and remove resources using the correct semantic method. Second, you will apply advanced requests features such as sessions, authentication, and proxies so your client can persist identity and route traffic securely. For example, sessions let you keep a login cookie across calls and reduce connection overhead. Third, you will inspect and interpret the response object: status code, headers, and JSON body. That means you can verify a successful operation and parse returned data for further processing. Finally on this screen you will begin to practice robust error handling: wrapping calls in try‑except blocks that catch timeouts, connection errors and HTTP errors so your program degrades gracefully instead of crashing. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can confirm you can perform the skill in a lab or assessment.

screens.title: Making a GET and reading the Response
screens.narratorSegment: A GET request is how you request a representation of a resource from a server. With requests, making a GET is intentionally simple: you call the library's get function with a URL, then inspect the returned response object. The response contains a numeric status code indicating success or error, headers that describe metadata such as content type, and the body which might be text or JSON. A key best practice is to call the response's raise_for_status method to convert HTTP error codes into exceptions, making your error handling clearer. Practically, you will often check the status code, then call the response json method to get a Python object. For example, a GET to a public user endpoint can return fields like name and repository counts; extracting them avoids string parsing. A common misconception is to assume that a 200 status guarantees the payload is valid for your needs; always validate fields after parsing. In short, get the response, raise on HTTP errors, parse JSON if expected, and validate the structure. Try a concrete example in the code panel to see these steps in practice and ask yourself: how will you validate the JSON your program depends on?

keyIdea.title: GET pattern
keyIdea.text: Call get, raise for HTTP errors, parse JSON, then validate the returned fields before trusting data.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › GET & Response
Definition
GET returns resource representations
  • Response includes status code, headers, body.
  • Use raise_for_status to convert bad status codes into exceptions.
  • Parse JSON with the response json method when Content-Type is application/json.
Example
A GET to a public user endpoint returning JSON you parse for name and public repository counts.
import requests

try:
    response = requests.get('https://api.github.com/users/octocat')
    response.raise_for_status()
    print('Status Code:', response.status_code)
    user_data = response.json()
    print('User Name:', user_data.get('name', 'N/A'))
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print('Request failed:', e)
Key Takeaway

Always check for HTTP errors before trusting response content and validate fields after parsing JSON.

Common Mistake

Assuming status code 200 means the payload matches your schema. Always check fields and types.

Check Your Understanding
  1. Why call raise_for_status before parsing?
  2. How would you confirm the JSON contains the keys you need?
Analogy
Think of raise_for_status as checking the envelope's stamp before reading the letter inside.

screens.title: POST, PUT and DELETE — choosing the right method
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP methods express intent. POST creates a new resource, PUT updates or creates a resource at a known location, and DELETE removes a resource. Choosing the right method keeps APIs predictable and avoids accidental side effects. When you send data, requests lets you provide it as form data via a data parameter or as JSON via a json parameter that encodes the body and sets the content type appropriately. As a concrete example, creating a new blog post uses POST with a JSON body containing title, body and userId; the server returns a new identifier. Updating the same post uses PUT to the resource URL with the changed fields. A frequent misconception is to use POST for all changes because it seems simpler; that loses the helpful semantics and can confuse A P I authors and clients. Always read the A P I contract. In practice, wrap these calls in try‑except blocks and call raise_for_status after the response. Consider idempotency: PUT is idempotent while POST typically is not, which affects retry logic. How will you choose methods in your next client?

keyIdea.title: Method semantics
keyIdea.text: Use POST to create, PUT to update or create at a known URL, and DELETE to remove; choose parameters to send JSON or form data as the API expects.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › POST / PUT / DELETE
POST — Create

Send a JSON body with the json parameter to create resources. The server usually returns a new id.

# Example: create a new post
post_data = {
  "title": "My New Blog Post",
  "body": "This is the content of my new post.",
  "userId": 1
}
# post_response = requests.post(url, json=post_data)
PUT — Update or Replace

Use PUT to update a resource at a known URL. PUT is idempotent: repeating it yields the same state.

# Example: update post id 1
# put_response = requests.put(f"{BASE_URL}/posts/1", json=updated_post_data)
DELETE — Remove

Delete removes the resource. Check the status code to confirm success; some APIs return no content.

# Example: delete post id 1
# delete_response = requests.delete(f"{BASE_URL}/posts/1")
Key Takeaway

Match the method to the intended action and consider idempotency when designing retries.

screens.title: Using requests.Session for persistent state
screens.narratorSegment: A session groups related requests and persists certain parameters between them. This is useful when you need a consistent User‑Agent header, want to reuse a login cookie, or simply want connection pooling for many calls to the same host. Using a session reduces overhead because the underlying TCP connection can be reused, which matters when making many requests in sequence. In practice you use a context manager pattern: open a session, update default headers, perform authentication if needed, then make subsequent requests that inherit those headers and cookies automatically. An important practice is to close the session when you are done; using a context manager ensures that. A common misconception is that a session is stateful like a browser — it stores cookies and headers but does not magically maintain application state beyond that. Use sessions for efficiency and convenience, and still design explicit authentication and token refresh logic when needed. The code panel shows a typical session pattern including a login then a request for a protected resource. Consider how you will store the custom headers and when to reuse sessions in your application.

keyIdea.title: Session benefits
keyIdea.text: Sessions persist headers and cookies and enable connection pooling, improving efficiency and simplifying repeated authenticated requests.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Sessions
Why use a Session?
  • Persist headers and cookies across requests without repeating code.
  • Connection pooling reuses TCP connections for the same host.
  • Use as a context manager to ensure resources are closed.
Pattern
with requests.Session() as session:
    session.headers.update({'User-Agent': 'MyApp/1.0'})
    login_response = session.post('https://example.com/login', data=login_payload)
    profile_response = session.get('https://example.com/profile')
    profile_response.raise_for_status()
    data = profile_response.json()
Key Takeaway

Use sessions to simplify repeated authenticated requests and improve performance through connection reuse.

Common Mistake

Recreating sessions for every request loses connection reuse benefits. Create a session per logical workflow instead.

Scenario
A background worker making many requests to the same API should reuse a session for efficiency; a short script that runs once may simply use requests directly.
Reflect: when will a session improve both security and performance in your services?

screens.title: Authentication strategies with requests
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication proves the client's identity to the server. requests supports simple patterns such as Basic Authentication where username and password are sent with each request, but modern APIs often prefer tokens or more sophisticated flows. For token based APIs you typically place the token in an Authorization header. The chapter notes that for complex OAuth flows you will usually rely on a complementary library that integrates with requests; this keeps your code focused on request logic while the dedicated library manages flows and token refresh. A crucial security point is not to hardcode credentials or tokens in source code; use environment variables or a secure configuration provider. A common misconception is that Basic Authentication is always insecure; while credentials travel with each request, when used over TLS it is protected in transit, but tokens or dedicated OAuth flows provide finer control for large distributed systems. In the code panel you can see a basic auth example. As a practical exercise, plan where your code will read credentials from and how tokens will be refreshed, because authentication is the gatekeeper to protected A P I operations.

keyIdea.title: Auth best practice
keyIdea.text: Prefer bearer tokens or OAuth for production APIs and never hardcode secrets; use secure storage and refresh strategies.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Authentication
Basic

Basic auth sends credentials with the request. Use it carefully and prefer TLS for transport security.

# Basic Auth example
response = requests.get('https://api.github.com/user', auth=('your_username', 'your_token'))
print(response.status_code)
Token / Header

Place tokens in an Authorization header via a session or per-request headers for bearer token schemes.

OAuth Note

For OAuth flows, use a library that integrates with requests to manage redirects and token refresh. Implement secure storage for tokens.

Key Takeaway

Never embed secrets in code. Use environment-based configuration and rotate tokens when possible.

screens.title: Proxies, timeouts and SSL verification
screens.narratorSegment: Network features affect both functionality and security. Proxies let you route requests through an intermediate server; requests accepts a proxies mapping so you can direct HTTP and HTTPS calls through the desired host. Be cautious: proxies can intercept traffic and should be trusted. Timeouts stop requests from hanging forever. Always set a timeout value so your application can recover or retry when a server is slow. The chapter demonstrates using a single timeout number or a pair for connect and read timeouts. SSL verification is on by default and should remain enabled in production to avoid man‑in‑the‑middle attacks. If you encounter certificate errors in controlled testing with self‑signed servers, you may use verify false, but that weakens security; instead provide a trusted CA bundle when possible. A common mistake is omitting timeouts and relying on default system behavior, which can block resources indefinitely. In practice, design timeouts appropriate for your environment and never disable SSL verification for production traffic. Consider logging timeout and SSL errors to inform operational responses. Proxies, timeouts and SSL verification means set timeouts, avoid untrusted proxies, and keep ssl verification enabled to protect integrity and avoid hangs.. In practical terms, network routing, preventing hangs, and certificate safety. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Network safety
keyIdea.text: Set timeouts, avoid untrusted proxies, and keep SSL verification enabled to protect integrity and avoid hangs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Proxies / Timeouts / SSL
Proxies

Define proxies to route traffic but avoid sending secrets through untrusted intermediaries.

proxies = {
  'http': 'http://10.10.1.10:3128',
  'https': 'http://10.10.1.10:1080',
}
response = requests.get('http://example.org', proxies=proxies)
Timeouts

Always set a timeout to avoid indefinite blocking. Use a single value or a connect/read tuple.

try:
    response = requests.get('http://example.com', timeout=5)
    response.raise_for_status()
except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
    print('Timed out after 5 seconds')
SSL Verification

Keep verification enabled in production. For controlled tests, you can disable it but prefer a custom CA bundle.

# Not recommended in production
response = requests.get('https://self-signed.example', verify=False)
Key Takeaway

Timeouts and SSL verification are essential runtime safety checks; proxies must be trusted before use.

screens.title: Streaming large downloads safely
screens.narratorSegment: Downloading large files can exhaust memory if you load the full response into memory. The most memory‑efficient pattern is to request the resource with streaming enabled so the client reads the body incrementally. With requests, use stream true and then iterate over response iter_content with a reasonable chunk size, writing each chunk directly to disk. This lets your program handle arbitrarily large files limited only by disk space, not R A M. The example in the chapter opens the response context manager, checks for HTTP errors, then writes in chunks to a file. A common mistake is to call response content which returns the entire body; that is fine for small payloads but dangerous for gigabyte scale. Another important detail is to choose a chunk size that balances system call overhead against memory use—8 kilobytes is a common default. Finally, set a longer timeout for large downloads and handle network interruptions with retries or resume logic where supported by the server. How will you test large file behavior in your environment? Streaming large downloads safely means use stream true and iter_content to write a response to disk in chunks, keeping memory usage low during large downloads.. In practical terms, avoid memory exhaustion with stream and chunked writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stream pattern
keyIdea.text: Use stream true and iter_content to write a response to disk in chunks, keeping memory usage low during large downloads.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Large File Downloads
Streaming workflow

Request with stream enabled, iterate chunks, write to disk, and always check raise_for_status first.

try:
    with requests.get('https://example.com/large_file.zip', stream=True, timeout=30) as r:
        r.raise_for_status()
        with open('large_file.zip', 'wb') as f:
            for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
                if chunk:
                    f.write(chunk)
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print('Download failed:', e)
Why it matters
Prevents excessive RAM use and lets you process or store very large assets safely.
Caveat

Use timeouts and consider resume support on unreliable networks to avoid restarting long downloads from zero.

Key Takeaway

stream true plus iter_content is the recommended pattern for large binary downloads.

screens.title: Robust error handling patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Network calls fail for many reasons: server errors, timeouts, DNS problems, or transient network blips. The requests library exposes exception types like HTTPError, ConnectionError and Timeout, and a common top-level RequestException for other issues. A robust pattern is to wrap network calls in try‑except blocks that catch specific exceptions when you need different recovery logic, and a general RequestException for logging and fallback. For HTTP errors use raise_for_status so that non‑2xx responses raise HTTPError and you can react to specific status codes like 401 or 429. For timeouts, retrying might help if the error is transient, but always limit retry attempts and add a delay so you do not overload the server. For connection errors, consider exponential backoff and give up after a bounded number of retries. Log full exception details for diagnostics, but avoid exposing secrets in logs. A common misconception is to catch all exceptions and silently continue; that hides operational problems. Instead, implement explicit recovery paths and sensible defaults so your application stays observable and resilient. How will you surface failures to your monitoring systems? Robust error handling patterns means catch specific requests exceptions, call raise_for_status for http errors, and design bounded retries and clear logging for operational visibility.. In practical terms, catching common requests exceptions and graceful degradation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Exception hierarchy
  • HTTPError — for 4xx and 5xx responses when raise_for_status is used.

    r.raise_for_status()

    # handle timeout

    # inspect he.response.status_code
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    # catch-all logging and fallback

Silently swallowing exceptions hides real problems; always log and surface errors for monitoring.

screens.title: Response object anatomy and inspection
screens.narratorSegment: The Response object is your window into the server's answer. It includes the status code, a headers mapping, a text representation and convenience methods like json that parse the body when appropriate. Understanding each component helps you respond correctly: status codes tell you success or failure; headers can indicate content type, caching, or server metadata; text gives raw body content for debugging; and json returns a parsed Python object when the payload is JSON. A common misstep is assuming json will always succeed; if the Content‑Type is not JSON or the payload is malformed, calling json can raise a ValueError. Therefore check headers or wrap parsing in try‑except to handle malformed responses. Use headers to decide how to treat payloads and sanitize any string content before logging to avoid leaking secrets. Also examine status codes beyond 200: 201 indicates creation, 204 indicates no content, and 4xx/5xx indicate client or server errors. Designing logic that branches on these signals makes your client robust and predictable. How will your code validate the structure of parsed JSON before using it? Starter Template (terminal demo)
import requests
import json

BASE_URL = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com'

def fetch_posts():
    print('--- Fetching Posts ---')
    try:
        response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/posts")
        response.raise_for_status()
        posts = response.json()
        print('First 5 post titles:')
        for i, post in enumerate(posts[:5]):

    with requests.Session() as session:

        print(f"Session User-Agent set: {session.headers['User-Agent']}")

screens.title: Security and operational best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond correct HTTP usage, operational practices determine whether your client remains secure and maintainable. Never hardcode credentials or A P I keys in source; instead use environment variables or a secrets manager. When logging, avoid printing entire response bodies or headers that may contain tokens. Instrument network calls with timing and status code metrics so your monitoring can alert on spikes in latency or error rates. When implementing retries, keep them bounded and consider idempotency: retries are safe for idempotent methods but risky for non‑idempotent ones. Respect SSL verification and only disable it in controlled test environments, preferring to supply a trusted certificate bundle for self‑signed servers. For large downloads, stream to disk and report progress to the user or logs. Finally, write small, focused functions for network interactions that return well‑documented results or error objects; this makes testing easier and reduces coupling. After following these patterns, your HTTP client will be more secure, observable, and resilient against real world issues. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to move from low‑level socket work to a practical, human‑friendly HTTP client using the requests library. You will see how a few lines of code handle connection details, status codes, headers and JSON payloads, and how higher‑level features like sessions, authentication, timeouts, and streaming keep your applications reliable. For example, a single GET call can return JSON you parse immediately, while a session preserves cookies and reuses TCP connections to speed repeated requests. We will also cover common pitfalls: never ignoring status codes, always setting sensible timeouts, and avoiding disabling SSL verification in production. Practical examples include interacting with a public testing A P I to create, update, and delete resources, and a safe pattern for downloading very large files without exhausting memory. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design an HTTP client that is secure, efficient, and resilient to network problems. Think of requests as the reliable bridge between your Python code and web services — what will you build with that bridge?

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when interacting with web services. First, you will master basic HTTP verbs and the common patterns for GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. Practically, that means you can fetch resources, create new ones, update existing records, and remove resources using the correct semantic method. Second, you will apply advanced requests features such as sessions, authentication, and proxies so your client can persist identity and route traffic securely. For example, sessions let you keep a login cookie across calls and reduce connection overhead. Third, you will inspect and interpret the response object: status code, headers, and JSON body. That means you can verify a successful operation and parse returned data for further processing. Finally on this screen you will begin to practice robust error handling: wrapping calls in try‑except blocks that catch timeouts, connection errors and HTTP errors so your program degrades gracefully instead of crashing. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can confirm you can perform the skill in a lab or assessment.

On this second objectives screen we make advanced concerns explicit so you can practice them in a lab. First, you will learn authentication patterns: how to include credentials or tokens safely and why you should avoid hardcoding secrets. A practical milestone is configuring a session with an Authorization header stored outside the code. Second, you will practice using proxies and understand the security tradeoffs. Use proxies only in controlled environments and avoid sending secrets through untrusted proxies. Third, you will master streaming and large downloads to preserve memory: reading in chunks rather than loading entire responses. Finally, we ask you to design a retry and fallback strategy for transient network errors. Even if we do not prescribe a specific library here, you will be able to implement retries reliably by catching network exceptions, limiting retry attempts, and adding delays between attempts. These capabilities let you build clients that work in the messy real world of unreliable networks.

A GET request is how you request a representation of a resource from a server. With requests, making a GET is intentionally simple: you call the library's get function with a URL, then inspect the returned response object. The response contains a numeric status code indicating success or error, headers that describe metadata such as content type, and the body which might be text or JSON. A key best practice is to call the response's raise_for_status method to convert HTTP error codes into exceptions, making your error handling clearer. Practically, you will often check the status code, then call the response json method to get a Python object. For example, a GET to a public user endpoint can return fields like name and repository counts; extracting them avoids string parsing. A common misconception is to assume that a 200 status guarantees the payload is valid for your needs; always validate fields after parsing. In short, get the response, raise on HTTP errors, parse JSON if expected, and validate the structure. Try a concrete example in the code panel to see these steps in practice and ask yourself: how will you validate the JSON your program depends on?

HTTP methods express intent. POST creates a new resource, PUT updates or creates a resource at a known location, and DELETE removes a resource. Choosing the right method keeps APIs predictable and avoids accidental side effects. When you send data, requests lets you provide it as form data via a data parameter or as JSON via a json parameter that encodes the body and sets the content type appropriately. As a concrete example, creating a new blog post uses POST with a JSON body containing title, body and userId; the server returns a new identifier. Updating the same post uses PUT to the resource URL with the changed fields. A frequent misconception is to use POST for all changes because it seems simpler; that loses the helpful semantics and can confuse A P I authors and clients. Always read the A P I contract. In practice, wrap these calls in try‑except blocks and call raise_for_status after the response. Consider idempotency: PUT is idempotent while POST typically is not, which affects retry logic. How will you choose methods in your next client?

A session groups related requests and persists certain parameters between them. This is useful when you need a consistent User‑Agent header, want to reuse a login cookie, or simply want connection pooling for many calls to the same host. Using a session reduces overhead because the underlying TCP connection can be reused, which matters when making many requests in sequence. In practice you use a context manager pattern: open a session, update default headers, perform authentication if needed, then make subsequent requests that inherit those headers and cookies automatically. An important practice is to close the session when you are done; using a context manager ensures that. A common misconception is that a session is stateful like a browser — it stores cookies and headers but does not magically maintain application state beyond that. Use sessions for efficiency and convenience, and still design explicit authentication and token refresh logic when needed. The code panel shows a typical session pattern including a login then a request for a protected resource. Consider how you will store the custom headers and when to reuse sessions in your application.

Authentication proves the client's identity to the server. requests supports simple patterns such as Basic Authentication where username and password are sent with each request, but modern APIs often prefer tokens or more sophisticated flows. For token based APIs you typically place the token in an Authorization header. The chapter notes that for complex OAuth flows you will usually rely on a complementary library that integrates with requests; this keeps your code focused on request logic while the dedicated library manages flows and token refresh. A crucial security point is not to hardcode credentials or tokens in source code; use environment variables or a secure configuration provider. A common misconception is that Basic Authentication is always insecure; while credentials travel with each request, when used over TLS it is protected in transit, but tokens or dedicated OAuth flows provide finer control for large distributed systems. In the code panel you can see a basic auth example. As a practical exercise, plan where your code will read credentials from and how tokens will be refreshed, because authentication is the gatekeeper to protected A P I operations.

Network features affect both functionality and security. Proxies let you route requests through an intermediate server; requests accepts a proxies mapping so you can direct HTTP and HTTPS calls through the desired host. Be cautious: proxies can intercept traffic and should be trusted. Timeouts stop requests from hanging forever. Always set a timeout value so your application can recover or retry when a server is slow. The chapter demonstrates using a single timeout number or a pair for connect and read timeouts. SSL verification is on by default and should remain enabled in production to avoid man‑in‑the‑middle attacks. If you encounter certificate errors in controlled testing with self‑signed servers, you may use verify false, but that weakens security; instead provide a trusted CA bundle when possible. A common mistake is omitting timeouts and relying on default system behavior, which can block resources indefinitely. In practice, design timeouts appropriate for your environment and never disable SSL verification for production traffic. Consider logging timeout and SSL errors to inform operational responses. Proxies, timeouts and SSL verification means set timeouts, avoid untrusted proxies, and keep ssl verification enabled to protect integrity and avoid hangs.. In practical terms, network routing, preventing hangs, and certificate safety. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Downloading large files can exhaust memory if you load the full response into memory. The most memory‑efficient pattern is to request the resource with streaming enabled so the client reads the body incrementally. With requests, use stream true and then iterate over response iter_content with a reasonable chunk size, writing each chunk directly to disk. This lets your program handle arbitrarily large files limited only by disk space, not R A M. The example in the chapter opens the response context manager, checks for HTTP errors, then writes in chunks to a file. A common mistake is to call response content which returns the entire body; that is fine for small payloads but dangerous for gigabyte scale. Another important detail is to choose a chunk size that balances system call overhead against memory use—8 kilobytes is a common default. Finally, set a longer timeout for large downloads and handle network interruptions with retries or resume logic where supported by the server. Beyond correct HTTP usage, operational practices determine whether your client remains secure and maintainable. Never hardcode credentials or A P I keys in source; instead use environment variables or a secrets manager. When logging, avoid printing entire response bodies or headers that may contain tokens. Instrument network calls with timing and status code metrics so your monitoring can alert on spikes in latency or error rates. When implementing retries, keep them bounded and consider idempotency: retries are safe for idempotent methods but risky for non‑idempotent ones. Respect SSL verification and only disable it in controlled test environments, preferring to supply a trusted certificate bundle for self‑signed servers. For large downloads, stream to disk and report progress to the user or logs. Finally, write small, focused functions for network interactions that return well‑documented results or error objects; this makes testing easier and reduces coupling.
